data.title: MONTGOMERY BUS BOYCOTT
data.subtitle: 381 Days of Courage, 1955–1956
data.introBody: December 1955, Montgomery, Alabama. Rosa Parks has been arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat. The Women's Political Council is printing leaflets by the thousands. Your neighbors are talking. You ride the Number 2 bus every morning to clean house for the Harrisons in the white neighborhood across town — and now you have pledged not to ride. Every day you must get to work another way, hold your job, and hold your community together.
data.trailFeedOpener: December 5, 1955: the empty buses roll past. Montgomery is watching.

events.title: Day One, Before Sunrise
events.text: It is still dark outside. Etta is on your porch, voice low, asking you to pass the word to the three women on Vine Street before they leave for the bus stop at six. You have worked for the Harrisons for eleven years. You have two children in school. Your husband's foreman has already made a remark about 'trouble.' Etta is watching your face.

choices.text: Tell Etta yes — you will go to the women on Vine Street before six.
choices.result: She chose to make her body part of the chain — to carry a message that could be traced back to her porch. Whatever happens next, she has answered Etta's question about who she is to her neighbors.

choices.text: Tell Etta you cannot do it — not because you disagree, but because you cannot put your household in that position.
choices.result: She chose to hold the boundary between solidarity and survival, between her neighbors' struggle and the people under her own roof who had no voice in the decision. She is not against the boycott; she is simply not willing to be its carrier.

events.title: The Empty Bus Rolls Past
events.text: It is early December and the first buses rattle by — almost entirely empty. A neighbor nudges you and smiles. But the walk to the Harrison house is four miles in the cold, and your feet already ache.
trivia: On December 5, 1955, more than 90 percent of Black bus riders stayed off the buses.
Jo Ann Robinson printed over 52,000 leaflets in a single night to spread the boycott call.

choices.text: Walk the whole way, head high.
choices.result: Your feet burn by the time you reach the Harrisons' door, but every neighbor you pass nods in recognition. You are one of the ones holding the line.

choices.text: Ask Mr. Dawson for a ride in his truck.
choices.result: Mr. Dawson is already taking three others. You squeeze in, and the cab smells like motor oil and hope. The community is building something together.

choices.text: Ride the bus just this once — no one will notice.
choices.result: You sit near the back. The driver doesn't look twice. But old Mrs. Gaines was watching from her porch, and by evening three people know.

events.title: Mass Meeting at Dexter Avenue
events.text: The MIA is holding a mass meeting at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church tonight. Dr. King will speak. Your husband says you look tired and should stay home — the children need you too.
events.imageSearchQuery: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church Montgomery Alabama
trivia: The Montgomery Improvement Association, led by Martin Luther King Jr., coordinated the boycott from Dexter Avenue Baptist Church.
Mass meetings gave boycotters information, inspiration, and a sense of collective strength.

choices.text: Go to the meeting — the community needs you there.
choices.result: The church is packed to the rafters. Dr. King's voice fills the hall. You come home late, but your heart is steadier than it's been in weeks. Your husband has already put the children to bed.

choices.text: Stay home with the children tonight.
choices.result: You tuck the children in and hear about the meeting secondhand the next morning. Your husband seems relieved. The movement will carry on without you tonight.

choices.text: Send word you'll donate a dollar to the carpool fund instead.
choices.result: It isn't the same as showing up, but the fund needs every coin. You compromise, and this time both sides of your life hold.

image.searchQuery: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church Montgomery Alabama

events.title: Mrs. Harrison Asks Questions
events.text: While you scrub the kitchen floor, Mrs. Harrison says casually that she has heard some of 'her' girls are involved in that boycott business. She is looking at the back of your head.
trivia: Many white employers threatened Black domestic workers with dismissal for participating in the boycott.
Some white employers offered to drive their workers to avoid losing household help, inadvertently aiding the boycott.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep scrubbing.
choices.result: Silence is its own answer. She doesn't press further, and you don't give her the satisfaction of your fear. Another day's pay secure.

choices.text: Tell her plainly you won't ride until it's fair.
choices.result: She stares at you for a long moment. 'I expected more sense from you,' she says, and leaves the room. The rest of the day is cold and silent. You spoke the truth in her house, and it cost you.

choices.text: Deflect — say you just prefer walking for your health.
choices.result: She makes a small sound that might be belief. The lie sits in your stomach all afternoon, but your job is safe for now.

events.title: The Carpool Is Full
events.text: The MIA carpool van is already packed when you reach the pickup point at six in the morning. Another woman — younger, with a long walk ahead of her — is standing in the cold beside you.
trivia: The MIA organized a sophisticated 40-station carpool network with over 300 private cars to replace the buses.
City officials tried to shut down the carpool by threatening insurance companies and arresting drivers on minor traffic violations.

choices.text: Give her your spot — you'll walk.
choices.result: She blinks in surprise and says thank you. You walk two hours in the cold and arrive late. Mrs. Harrison docks you twenty minutes' pay. You don't regret it.

choices.text: Take your spot — you were here first.
choices.result: You get to work on time. The younger woman is still standing there as the van pulls away. You tell yourself you had no choice. The thought follows you all day.

choices.text: Wait and try to flag down the next private car.
choices.result: A church deacon stops fifteen minutes later. You're only slightly late. Not a heroic morning, but a survivable one.

events.title: Dr. King's House Is Bombed
events.text: Word reaches your block before breakfast: Dr. King's home was bombed last night. His wife and baby daughter were inside — both survived. Montgomery's Black community is gathering in the street.
trivia: Martin Luther King Jr.'s home on Jackson Street was bombed on January 30, 1956.
King urged the crowd gathered outside his home to respond with nonviolence, saying 'We cannot solve this problem through retaliatory violence.'

choices.text: Go stand with the crowd outside the church.
choices.result: Hundreds of people are already there. Dr. King himself appears on his porch and asks everyone to go home peacefully. You hear the tremor in his voice and go home believing him.

choices.text: Stay inside — it isn't safe in the street.
choices.result: Your husband locks the front door and prays with the children. You sit together in the back room listening to distant voices. The community holds without you tonight.

choices.text: Keep your head down and go to work anyway.
choices.result: You arrive on time. Mrs. Harrison seems surprised to see you. On the walk home you pass the gathered crowd and none of your neighbors can quite meet your eyes.

events.title: The Last Hard Morning
events.text: It is November 1956. The Supreme Court has ruled bus segregation unconstitutional, but the order has not reached Montgomery yet. Your neighbors are debating: ride early as a statement, or hold the line until the official order arrives and make the victory complete.
trivia: On November 13, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed a lower court ruling in Browder v. Gayle, declaring Alabama's bus segregation laws unconstitutional.
The Montgomery Bus Boycott officially ended on December 20, 1956, when the federal desegregation order arrived in Montgomery.

choices.text: Hold the line until the written order arrives.
choices.result: A few neighbors ride in the first days and face violence — rocks through windows, a sniper's bullet grazing a passenger. Your discipline, and theirs, ensures the victory lands intact. December 20th comes. The order is here. You walk to the stop and board the bus in the front door.

choices.text: Ride now — the ruling is enough, and your feet have suffered long enough.
choices.result: You sit where you choose. It feels extraordinary for about thirty seconds, then frightening — a white man boards and the driver watches you both. You get to work fine. You also hear, later, that three boycotters were attacked this week. The movement needed those extra weeks of discipline.

choices.text: Wait and watch what the church elders decide.
choices.result: The elders say hold the line. You hold it. The decision was made for you, and you followed it without having to choose. When the order arrives you board the bus with everyone else. It means the same thing — almost.

events.title: Week Three — A Neighbor Is Fired

text.default: Word comes down Vine Street that one of the women you spoke to before dawn has lost her job. Her employer found out she had been talking. You do not know if your name came up. You sit with that uncertainty the way you sit with a stone in your shoe — it does not stop you walking, but you feel it every step. At church on Sunday she grips your hand and does not let go for a long time. You are not sure whether that means she forgives you or whether forgiveness is even the right word for what passes between you.

Word comes down Vine Street that one of the women there has lost her job. She organized on her own — you were not part of it. You feel the relief and the shame of the relief in the same breath. At church on Sunday she sits two pews ahead of you and you watch the back of her head and try to decide whether what you did was protect your family or simply protect yourself, and you find you cannot fully separate the two.

text.default: The buses are still empty. You have been walking, catching rides, arriving tired and sometimes late. The Harrisons have said nothing yet, but the silence has a temperature to it. You do not know if you will have this job in a month. What you know is that when Etta knocked on your door before sunrise, you answered. That is a thing that happened. It does not solve anything, but it is a fact about who you are, and you are learning to live inside it.

The buses are still empty. You have been walking, catching rides, arriving tired and sometimes late — the same as everyone else, regardless of what you said or did not say on that dark porch three weeks ago. The boycott did not need you to carry its message. That is true. You turn it over and over. It is true, and it does not entirely settle the question you have been sitting with since before sunrise on the first day.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Claudette Colvin
sages.title: Student and Boycott Plaintiff, Browder v. Gayle
sages.bio: Claudette Colvin was fifteen years old when she was arrested on a Montgomery bus in March 1955 — nine months before Rosa Parks. She later became one of four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal lawsuit that ultimately struck down bus segregation.

sages.advice: "The lawyers needed plaintiffs who would hold up in court. I was fifteen and unmarried — they worried about me. But I didn't go away. The case needed us both: the boycott and the lawsuit, together."

data.historicalContext: The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted 381 days, from December 5, 1955, to December 20, 1956. It ended when the Supreme Court's ruling in Browder v. Gayle, declaring Alabama's bus segregation unconstitutional, was formally delivered to Montgomery. The boycott did not erase Jim Crow from the South — years of struggle, violence, legislation, and sacrifice followed. But it proved that organized, sustained, nonviolent economic pressure could crack legal segregation, and it launched Martin Luther King Jr. onto the national stage. The women who walked miles every day to their jobs — domestic workers, laundresses, maids — supplied the boycott's real economic force. Their names were not in the newspapers. Their feet were on the pavement.

verdict.good: You walked when you could have ridden. You spoke when silence was safer. You gave up your seat in the carpool van and arrived late, and you did it more than once. None of it was free — Mrs. Harrison watched you with narrowed eyes, your husband worried in the evenings, and your feet hurt every day of the 381. The boycott broke bus segregation. Rosa Parks was vindicated. Claudette Colvin was vindicated. The women who walked those miles were vindicated. History recorded the names of the leaders. It did not record yours. You were there anyway.
verdict.bad: You calculated every choice and came out ahead — on time to work, money in your purse, Mrs. Harrison satisfied. When your neighbors needed the carpool seat you were already in it. When the mass meeting called, you stayed home. The boycott won without your sacrifice, which means you got the same integrated bus as the woman who walked four miles in the cold every morning for a year. You can tell yourself the movement didn't need you. It didn't. But it asked, and every time it asked, you looked the other way.
verdict.indifferent: You moved through 381 days and let others make the hard calls. You followed the elders when they decided and waited to see what the crowd would do. You never crossed the line — not on purpose. You just never quite stepped up to it either. The boycott happened around you. The bombed porch, the packed church, the woman standing in the cold at the carpool stop — you saw it all and passed through it without it costing you anything, because you never offered anything. The buses were desegregated. You boarded like everyone else. Someone else paid for that seat.

data.reviewSummary: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, an NAACP secretary and seamstress, was arrested on a Montgomery, Alabama city bus for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. That same night, Jo Ann Robinson, president of the Women's Political Council, used Alabama State College mimeograph machines to print more than 52,000 leaflets calling for a one-day bus boycott. E. D. Nixon, the Montgomery NAACP chapter leader and Pullman Porter, posted Parks's bail and convened Black ministers who formed the Montgomery Improvement Association. They elected twenty-six-year-old Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. as president. The single day became 381. Black riders — roughly 75 percent of Montgomery City Lines' revenue — stayed off the buses. Domestic workers, who made up the largest share of daily riders, walked miles each morning to white neighborhoods rather than pay a fare. The MIA organized a 40-station carpool network using over 300 private cars to keep people moving. City officials fought back by arresting carpool drivers on minor traffic violations and pressuring insurance companies to cancel policies on carpool vehicles. On January 30, 1956, King's home was bombed while his wife and infant daughter were inside; both survived, and King urged the crowd that gathered to respond with nonviolence. Claudette Colvin had been arrested nine months before Parks, in March 1955, for the same act of refusal. Though community leaders waited for a more favorable case before acting, Colvin became one of four plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal lawsuit that challenged Alabama's bus segregation laws. On November 13, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the lower court's ruling in Browder v. Gayle, declaring bus segregation unconstitutional. The boycott officially ended on December 20, 1956, when the federal desegregation order arrived in Montgomery — 381 days after it began. The women who walked those miles were the economic engine of the movement. The victory belonged to everyone who held the line.

data.title: THE STAR-SPANGLED WAR
data.subtitle: An American Naval Officer, 1807–1815
data.introBody: 1807. You are a U.S. Navy lieutenant stationed in the Chesapeake Bay. Britain and France are at war, and the Royal Navy treats American ships as their personal recruiting grounds. You have your commission, your pay, and your reputation — and all three are about to be tested.
data.trailFeedOpener: Spring 1807: your sloop rides at anchor in the Chesapeake Roads. A British man-of-war shadows you on the horizon.

resourceLabels.payPrizeMoney: Cash on hand — your accumulated naval pay and any prize shares from captured vessels.
resourceLabels.officerReputation: Your standing among the Navy's officers, your crew, and the public — the honor that opens doors and earns trust.
resourceLabels.physicalCondition: Your body's endurance after months of wet decks, poor rations, cannon fire, and sleepless watches.

events.title: ACT I — The Chesapeake Roads, early patrol, before war is declared
events.text: A British sloop-of-war comes alongside under a 'right of search' claim. Your captain is ashore at the moment of the boarding; you are the senior officer on deck. The press-gang produces no lawful warrant under American law, but they hold naval commission and a muster list. They move toward John Cody — a Baltimore waterman you personally recruited, a man holding a notarized protection certificate. The British lieutenant meets your eyes. Your crew watches. Whatever you do in the next thirty seconds will define you to them — and to yourself — for the rest of this war.

choices.text: Step between Cody and the press-gang, declare his citizenship aloud to both crews, and formally refuse the seizure on the record.
choices.result: The lieutenant has decided that the dignity of a citizen is not something an officer can defer — that the republic's honor lives in individual acts of resistance, not in patient diplomacy. He has made himself the embodiment of the grievance that is driving the nation to war, and he will carry that identity forward as a man who believes authority must be checked from below.

choices.text: Hold your position, order your crew to stand easy, and enter the seizure in the ship's log in precise legal language — a formal record, but no physical confrontation.
choices.result: The lieutenant has decided that the republic is best served by institutions that outlast any single man's suffering — that logging an outrage and surviving to fight through proper channels is itself a form of patriotism. He will carry forward the identity of a man who believes order and restraint are not betrayal but the slow sinew of a lasting navy.

events.title: War is Declared
events.text: June 1812. Word reaches the harbor: Congress has declared war on Britain. Henry Clay and the War Hawks got their vote. Your ship is ordered to sea immediately — but half your crew is unpaid for three months.
trivia: Congress declared war on Britain on June 18, 1812.
Henry Clay of Kentucky led the War Hawk faction pushing for war over impressment and frontier grievances.

choices.text: Demand the paymaster settle the crew before sailing.
choices.result: The men get their coin — and you earn their loyalty. Your captain calls it insubordinate. It costs you.

choices.text: Order the crew to sea on the Navy's promise.
choices.result: The men obey and grumble below decks. Your captain approves. The crew remembers.

choices.text: Note the pay arrears in your log and sail.
choices.result: You document it properly and do nothing more. The crew sees a man who follows procedures.

image.artist: Julian Vannerson or Montgomery P. Simons

events.title: A Prize Taken
events.text: Your vessel intercepts a British merchant brig. She strikes her colors. Prize money will follow — but your first lieutenant wants to strip her cargo now, before the Admiralty court can assess it.
trivia: Prize money from captured enemy ships was divided among the crew by rank, with officers receiving the largest shares.
Looting before a prize court ruling was illegal and could forfeit the entire award.

choices.text: Follow prize law. Send her to court untouched.
choices.result: The court condemns the brig. Your share arrives months later — smaller than theft, larger than nothing. Your crew respects the rule.

choices.text: Allow the first lieutenant his cut. Look away.
choices.result: The money is real and arrives fast. If the Navy ever inquires, you have no clean answer.

choices.text: Take only your own fair share and say nothing.
choices.result: You are not the worst man present, but you are not clean either.

events.title: The Capital Burns
events.text: August 1814. Admiral Cockburn's redcoats march into Washington unopposed. The Capitol and White House are in flames. Dolley Madison has fled — but witnesses say she stopped long enough to save the portrait of Washington. You are ordered to defend the naval yard or torch it yourself.
trivia: Admiral George Cockburn directed the burning of Washington on August 24–25, 1814.
Dolley Madison famously saved the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington as British troops advanced.
American commanders ordered the Washington Navy Yard burned to prevent its capture — a painful but deliberate act.

sageAdvice.name: Dolley Madison
sageAdvice.line: Save what cannot be replaced. Property can be rebuilt; symbols of the republic cannot.

sageAdvice.name: Admiral Cockburn
sageAdvice.line: Your capital is proof that this republic cannot defend itself.

choices.text: Fire the yard yourself before the British reach it.
choices.result: You put the torch to your own work. Cockburn finds ashes. It is the right thing and it breaks something in you.

choices.text: Abandon the yard and join the retreat south.
choices.result: The yard falls intact to Cockburn's men. Your name appears in a dispatch you do not want read aloud.

choices.text: Wait for orders that never come, then withdraw.
choices.result: You waited for the chain of command and the chain of command fled. The yard is lost by indecision.

events.title: Bombs over Fort McHenry
events.text: September 13–14, 1814. The Royal Navy pounds Fort McHenry for 25 hours. Major Armistead's garrison holds. You are aboard a support vessel close enough to hear every burst. A wounded sailor needs you to carry him below — but your gun crew is one man short.
trivia: The British bombardment of Fort McHenry lasted about 25 hours, from September 13 to 14, 1814.
Major George Armistead commanded the 1,000-man garrison that held Fort McHenry.
Francis Scott Key witnessed the bombardment from a British vessel and wrote the poem that became the national anthem.

sageAdvice.name: Major George Armistead
sageAdvice.line: If the flag is still flying at dawn, we have won something that no dispatch can fully say.

sageAdvice.name: Francis Scott Key
sageAdvice.line: I watched from their deck all night. When the rockets' red glare showed the flag still there — I have never felt such a thing.

choices.text: Carry the wounded man below yourself.
choices.result: The man lives. Your gun crew managed without you. Your back carries the cost for weeks.

choices.text: Leave him and stay at the gun.
choices.result: The gun keeps firing. The man dies before anyone can reach him. Fort McHenry holds. You remember his face.

choices.text: Call for a surgeon and hold your post.
choices.result: The surgeon is busy with three others. The man waits too long. You did everything correctly except the one thing that mattered.

events.title: The Flag Still There at Dawn
events.text: As the bombardment ceases, a lawyer named Francis Scott Key — held on a British vessel during the battle — asks to speak with you on deck. He has written something down. The garrison's enormous flag, thirty feet by forty-two, is still flying over McHenry. Key's hands are shaking.
trivia: Francis Scott Key wrote 'The Star-Spangled Banner' after witnessing the bombardment from the British ship HMS Tonnant.
The flag that flew over Fort McHenry measured 30 by 42 feet and was made by Mary Pickersgill of Baltimore.
events.leaveText: Return to your duties. Leave Key to his poem.

attempts.buttonText: Ask Key to read you the first verse.
attempts.successText: He reads it quietly. Something in the words settles the exhaustion in your chest.
attempts.failureText: Key's voice breaks. Neither of you say anything for a long moment. That silence costs you.

attempts.buttonText: Tell Key what you saw from the gun deck.
attempts.successText: He adds a detail you gave him. His pen scratches it in. You are, briefly, part of something permanent.
attempts.failureText: He is not ready to hear more. You have pushed into a private grief.

attempts.buttonText: Ask Key to sign a copy for you to keep.
attempts.successText: He signs it. You fold it into your jacket. You will carry it home.
attempts.failureText: He hesitates — not sure this is the moment for souvenirs. You feel the smallness of the request.

events.title: The Treaty and What Comes After
events.text: December 1814. The Treaty of Ghent ends the war — impressment is not even mentioned in its terms. Sailors who suffered for this cause got no formal remedy. A young officer from your own crew asks you, directly: was it worth it? Your answer will follow you home.
trivia: The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, restored pre-war boundaries and said nothing about impressment.
Though neither side won decisive territorial gains, the war established American sovereignty and national identity — and impressment ended in practice because the Napoleonic Wars had ended.

choices.text: Tell him honestly: the treaty settled nothing — but we proved something.
choices.result: The men who hear you nod slowly. Your family, reading your letter, hears the distance between you and home and does not know when it will close.

choices.text: Tell him it was worth it — say what he needs to hear.
choices.result: He seems satisfied. You know you gave him comfort, not truth. You are already thinking of shore leave and home.

choices.text: Tell him the Navy will explain when orders come down.
choices.result: He looks at you for a moment and walks back to his post. You gave him a bureaucratic answer to a human question.

events.title: ACT II — After the USS Chesapeake engagement; survivors are being mustered and the crew looks to you for meaning

text.default: The men who saw you step forward for Cody are here — some of them. Others are not. They remember what you did on the Roads, and they square it against today's dead. One of your surviving sailors says nothing, only looks at you the way a man looks at a promise he is not sure was worth keeping. You gave them a lieutenant who would not flinch — and now they are measuring whether that refusal to flinch brought them to this deck or saved them from something worse.

One of your surviving sailors says nothing, only looks at you the way a man looks at a promise he is not sure was worth keeping. You gave them a lieutenant who would not flinch — and now they are measuring whether that refusal to flinch brought them to this deck or saved them from something worse.

The log entry you wrote about Cody's seizure was copied into a congressional report. A lawyer in Washington cited it. That fact is cold comfort here. The men look at you and remember that you ordered them to stand easy once before when standing easy felt like surrender. They do not say it aloud, but the question is in the air: will you order them to stand easy again? You have been careful and correct and present. You wonder, in the silence after the muster, whether careful and correct is something the dead would recognize as loyalty.

choices.text: Go on.

events.title: ACT III — The night watch after the bombardment of Fort McHenry; the flag is still there; the war's meaning is being spoken aloud by the men

text.default: The crew speaks of the flag as proof — proof that resistance, direct and personal and costly, is the only language a young republic can speak to an empire. You hear Cody's name in the conversation, though he is not here. You were the first sentence of the argument they are finishing tonight. You wonder if the argument was worth its price, and you find you cannot be sure — only that you could not have been yourself and spoken any other first word.

The crew speaks of the flag as proof — proof that patient endurance, discipline held under humiliation, is what kept a navy together long enough to fight. You think of the log entry, the copies made, the citations. You think of Cody, whom you did not save, whose name is in a record that helped produce this war. The flag is there. You are not sure what you owe it, or what it owes you. You know only that the young republic is still here, and so are you, and you are not certain whether those two facts are connected or simply simultaneous.

sages.name: Henry Clay
sages.title: War Hawk Congressman from Kentucky

portraitAttribution.artist: Julian Vannerson or Montgomery P. Simons

sages.bio: Henry Clay of Kentucky was the most forceful voice demanding war with Britain. As Speaker of the House, he channeled fury over impressment and frontier grievances into a declaration of war in June 1812.
sages.greeting: You meet Clay in a Washington tavern before the declaration. He fixes you with bright, certain eyes and speaks before you sit down.
sages.advice: "The British treat your sailors as their property. Every man dragged off an American deck is an insult to the republic's sovereignty. The time for petitions is done."

question.question: What was the primary stated grievance that led Congress to declare war on Britain in 1812?
choices: Britain refused to sell manufactured goods to the United States
Britain was seizing American sailors and forcing them into the Royal Navy
Britain had invaded and occupied American cities along the frontier
Britain refused to recognize American independence
question.explanation: Impressment — the Royal Navy stopping American ships and forcing sailors they claimed as British subjects into service — was the central grievance. Between 1803 and 1812, thousands of American sailors were seized. This violated American sovereignty and enraged both the public and Congress.
question.teksRef: 8.5(A) — Causes of the War of 1812 including impressment

sages.name: Dolley Madison
sages.title: First Lady and preserver of national symbols
sages.bio: When Admiral Cockburn's troops marched on Washington in August 1814, Dolley Madison refused to leave the Executive Mansion until she had secured the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington — saving one of the republic's defining symbols from British torches.
sages.greeting: You encounter Mrs. Madison in the chaotic hours before the capital falls. She is calm in a way that makes every panicking official around her look small.
sages.advice: "I sent the silver ahead and the papers after. The portrait of General Washington I would not leave. Some things must not be taken from us."

question.question: What did Dolley Madison save when she fled the White House before British troops arrived in 1814?
choices: The original Declaration of Independence
The Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington
President Madison's war dispatches
The White House silver service
question.explanation: Dolley Madison famously ensured that the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington was removed from the wall and carried to safety before she fled. The British burned the White House and Capitol shortly after. The portrait became a symbol of what the republic refused to surrender.
question.teksRef: 8.5(B) — The burning of Washington and the defense of national symbols

sages.name: James Madison
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: James Madison led the republic into its first war since independence, watched his capital burn, and signed the Treaty of Ghent — a peace that restored the pre-war status quo without formally resolving impressment, yet established that the United States had survived its trial as a sovereign nation.
sages.greeting: You are granted a brief audience with the President in the weeks after Ghent. He looks older than the portraits. He speaks carefully, as if measuring every word for history.
sages.advice: "The treaty does not name every grievance we carried into this war. But the world now knows we will fight. That, Lieutenant, may be the whole of what we needed to prove."

question.question: What was the key outcome of the Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814?
choices: Britain formally agreed to stop impressment of American sailors
The United States gained Canada as a territory
The war ended with borders restored to pre-war lines — impressment was not addressed
Britain paid reparations for ships seized during the war
question.explanation: The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, essentially returned both sides to the status quo before the war — no territory changed hands, and impressment was never formally addressed. Yet the war's outcome demonstrated that the young republic could defend its sovereignty, and impressment ended in practice because the Napoleonic Wars had also ended.

data.historicalContext: The War of 1812 ended in December 1814 with the Treaty of Ghent, which restored pre-war boundaries and never formally addressed impressment. Roughly 2,260 Americans died in battle; thousands more in disease. The Republic survived, the capital was rebuilt, and Fort McHenry's defense produced 'The Star-Spangled Banner.' The war's most lasting outcome was psychological: a young nation had faced the world's greatest naval power and not broken.

verdict.good: You stood for the sailors who had no voice, burned what needed burning so the enemy couldn't have it, and told the truth when comfort would have been easier. The Treaty of Ghent said nothing about impressment — the formal injustice was never remedied. But the men who served with you knew what you were, and that knowledge traveled. The republic survived, barely. You helped hold it together, at real cost to yourself. That is the only ledger that matters.
verdict.bad: You found the profitable side of each choice and stood on it. The pay that wasn't yours, the yard you didn't burn, the easy word instead of the true one — each time you kept something for yourself and gave nothing back. The war ended with no clear winner and no formal remedy for the sailors whose suffering started it. You came home ahead of most. The men who were dragged off American decks into British service got nothing from the treaty either. You had more to offer than you gave.
verdict.indifferent: You were present for all of it — the declarations, the burning, the bombardment, the treaty — and you took the path that asked the least at every turn. Not corrupt, not cowardly, just perpetually elsewhere when the weight had to be carried by someone. The War of 1812 asked the young republic whether it was real enough to fight for. You passed through that question without ever answering it. The flag was still there at dawn. You had nothing to do with it.

data.reviewSummary:
The conflict that became the War of 1812 grew from years of British impressment — the Royal Navy's practice of boarding American merchant ships and forcing sailors they claimed as British subjects into service. American sailors carried notarized protection certificates to prove their citizenship, but the Royal Navy routinely ignored them. By 1812, Henry Clay of Kentucky and the War Hawk faction had channeled this outrage into a declaration of war, passed by Congress on June 18, 1812. Clay argued that impressment was a direct assault on American sovereignty and that petitions had accomplished nothing. Congress agreed, though the country was deeply divided.

At sea, U.S. Navy officers navigated prize law alongside combat. When an enemy vessel was captured and condemned by a prize court, its value was divided among the crew by rank — a major financial incentive, and a system that could be corrupted if officers helped themselves before the court could assess the prize.

The war's darkest hour came in August 1814 when Admiral George Cockburn led British forces into Washington, burning the Capitol and the White House on August 24–25. Before fleeing, Dolley Madison ensured that the Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington was removed from the White House and carried to safety — refusing to let a defining national symbol be taken. American commanders ordered the Washington Navy Yard burned themselves, rather than let it fall intact to Cockburn.

British forces then moved on Baltimore. The Royal Navy bombarded Fort McHenry for approximately 25 hours, from September 13 to September 14, 1814, firing over 1,500 shells. Major George Armistead's garrison of roughly 1,000 men held. The fort's garrison flag — measuring 30 by 42 feet, sewn by Mary Pickersgill of Baltimore — was still flying at dawn. A lawyer named Francis Scott Key, held aboard a British vessel under a flag of truce, watched the entire bombardment from the enemy's deck. He wrote the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'

The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, ended the war by restoring pre-war boundaries. It said nothing about impressment. Neither side gained territory. Yet the war established that the young American republic could survive a major foreign threat and defend its sovereignty — and the Napoleonic Wars ended shortly after, removing the demand for sailors that had driven impressment in the first place.

data.title: THE THIRD CRUSADE
data.subtitle: Acre to Jerusalem, 1191–1192
data.introBody: You have taken the cross and sailed with Richard's fleet to the Holy Land. The siege of Acre grinds on — heat, disease, Saracen arrows. What you do here, and how you do it, will define the man you carry home.
data.trailFeedOpener: Summer 1191: the host anchors off Acre. The walls have held for two years. You step ashore into a camp that smells of rot and smoke.

resourceLabels.honour: Your standing among knights and God

data.historicalContext: The Third Crusade (1189–1192) was launched after Saladin's forces captured Jerusalem in 1187. Richard I of England and Philip II of France led the combined crusading host to the Holy Land. After a grinding siege, Acre fell in July 1191. Richard's disciplined coastal march defeated Saladin at Arsuf. Two approaches to Jerusalem failed. The campaign ended with the Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192: pilgrims gained access to Jerusalem, but the city remained in Muslim hands. Richard never took Jerusalem. He sailed home in October 1192, captured by the Duke of Austria, and ransomed. The crusade is remembered for the brilliance and brutality of both commanders, and for the massacre of 2,700 prisoners at Ayyadieh.

events.title: The walls of Acre have held for weeks. A sortie from the garrison has killed three men from your company, including a boy you were responsible for. Word comes down from the commanders: prisoners taken in the next engagement are to be held pending negotiations over the True Cross and ransoms. That night your company captures a Saracen scout — alone, lightly armed, clearly not a soldier. Your sergeant wants to execute him before dawn so he cannot carry intelligence back. The chaplain attached to your company reminds you that you took the cross to fight for the Lord, not to become murderers of scouts. Your lord will not hear of it either way; the decision is yours to make quietly and live with.
events.text: A lone Saracen prisoner, the sergeant's pragmatic case for killing him, the chaplain's invocation of the vow, and the memory of the boy who died in the sortie — all pressing at once in the dark outside the walls of Acre.

choices.text: You hold the prisoner and bind him. Whatever he knows, whatever he costs to keep, you will not execute a bound man. The vow said something about what you would be, and you are going to hold it.
choices.result: The knight draws a line in the mud at Acre. He is not naive — he knows the cost — but he refuses to let the campaign dissolve the covenant into pure utility. The vow is not an excuse for what he does; it is a constraint on it. This makes him a particular kind of man: one who will carry the tension of a war that does not reward that choice.

choices.text: You turn away and let the sergeant do what needs doing. The crusade is too large, too costly, and too holy in its purpose to be lost for scruple over one scout. God will understand what this war requires.
choices.result: The knight lets the campaign rewrite the vow's content. He does not stop believing; he does not stop fighting. But the sacred frame has become retrospective blessing rather than prospective constraint. He is now a man who does what the crusade requires and calls it God's work — which is exactly the logic that produced every atrocity on this march.

events.title: Siege Duty at Acre
events.text: The engineers need knights to supervise overnight shifts on the siege lines — hauling stones for the mangonels, shoring up approach trenches under arrow-fire. It is exhausting, dangerous, and unglamorous.
trivia: Medieval siege engines called mangonels hurled stones weighing up to 300 pounds at city walls.
Dysentery and fever killed more crusaders at Acre than Saracen weapons.

choices.text: Take the overnight shift yourself.
choices.result: Your men see you in the trench beside them. The shift is brutal and the dawn finds you hollow-eyed — but the mangonel is in place.

choices.text: Assign it to the men-at-arms; rest yourself.
choices.result: You sleep. The shift is done well enough. But the men notice you were not there, and the sergeant says nothing, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Negotiate a shared rotation among the knights.
choices.result: Fair enough, and it works. No one is ruined by it, no one is especially honoured by it.

events.title: Philip's Demands
events.text: Philip II's officers are requisitioning supplies from English-aligned knights for the French contingent. Philip claims treaty rights. Richard's steward calls it theft. You have rations your own men need for a week.
trivia: Philip II of France and Richard I were uneasy allies — rivals at home who needed each other in the Holy Land.
The crusading coalition depended on shared supply lines, but national contingents guarded their own stores jealously.

choices.text: Hand over half your stores to keep the peace.
choices.result: It costs you. Your men eat shorter rations for three days. But the alliance holds a little longer, and Philip's officers nod at you with something that might be respect.

choices.text: Refuse. Your men come first.
choices.result: Your men eat well. Philip's steward marks your name. The fracture between the kings widens, and you have added your small weight to it.

choices.text: Refer Philip's officers to Richard's quartermaster.
choices.result: A sensible answer that solves nothing and offends no one today. The same dispute will reappear tomorrow.

events.title: Acre Falls — The Garrison Surrenders
events.text: The walls of Acre finally crack on 12 July 1191. The garrison surrenders to Richard and Philip. The crusaders flood into the city. Some men are already looting. A Genoese merchant offers to buy any valuables you can bring out of the citadel stores.
trivia: Acre was one of the most important ports in the Levant — whoever held it controlled supply lines into the Holy Land.
After Acre fell, Philip II of France departed for home almost immediately, leaving Richard in sole command.

choices.text: Keep discipline; forbid your men to loot.
choices.result: Your men grumble loudly and one deserts to join the free-for-all. But when Richard's officers come looking for reliable captains for garrison duty, your name is offered.

choices.text: Sell valuables to the Genoese merchant.
choices.result: Your purse is heavy. Your men share a cut and call you shrewd. A clerk records the sale in a ledger you will not see again, but it exists.

choices.text: Stand aside — let the men do as they will.
choices.result: You neither lead nor prevent. The men take what they take. You come away a little richer and a little smaller.

events.title: The March South — Hold the Line
events.text: On the coastal march Richard's order is absolute: no knight breaks formation to chase Saracen riders, no matter the provocation. The Ayyubid cavalry have been feathering the column for three days. A knight beside you breaks rank and charges. His horse goes down. He is surrounded.
trivia: Richard's march from Acre to Jaffa was considered a masterpiece of medieval military discipline — the army moved in a tight formation that Saladin's cavalry could not break.
At the Battle of Arsuf, the Hospitaller knights finally broke rank after hours of provocation, forcing Richard to order a general charge that won the battle.

choices.text: Break rank and ride to pull him out.
choices.result: You drag him free. Two horses are lost and Richard's formation officer is furious. The rescued knight will follow you anywhere. Your body pays for a week.

choices.text: Hold position. Orders are orders.
choices.result: You watch him die. The formation holds. Richard's discipline is what got the army this far. You know that. It does not help.

choices.text: Shout for a Hospitaller to retrieve him.
choices.result: A Hospitaller sergeant rides out and pulls the man clear — barely. You stayed in line. It was a sensible compromise. He would probably have done the same for you.

events.title: Jaffa — Al-Adil Sends an Envoy
events.text: At Jaffa, Saladin's brother Al-Adil meets Richard's envoys. A back-channel message reaches your billet: Al-Adil seeks a minor knight as witness to informal talks — someone trustworthy on both sides. It is not glamorous. It may come to nothing.
trivia: Al-Adil, known to crusaders as Saphadin, acted as Saladin's chief diplomatic intermediary throughout the Third Crusade.
Richard I and Al-Adil conducted unconventional personal diplomacy — Richard even proposed a political marriage between Al-Adil and his sister Joan, though it came to nothing.

choices.text: Volunteer. You will serve as witness.
choices.result: The talks are long and inconclusive, conducted through translators in a tent that smells of smoke and cardamom. Nothing is decided. But Al-Adil's secretary makes a note of your name.

choices.text: Decline. You are a soldier, not a diplomat.
choices.result: A sensible answer. Another knight takes the post. You rest. Nothing changes.

events.title: The Hill of the Holy City
events.text: You can see Jerusalem from this hill. Richard has turned back — the army cannot hold the city even if it takes it. A small company of pilgrims insists on pressing forward despite orders; some are men you have marched beside for a year. You must decide now what this campaign was for.
trivia: Richard I came within sight of Jerusalem twice but refused to advance, judging that even a captured city could not be held with the forces available.
The Treaty of Jaffa, signed September 1192, allowed Christian pilgrims access to Jerusalem without retaking it militarily.

choices.text: Go with them. You took the cross for this.
choices.result: You reach the walls. You pray. You come back alive, barely, without orders, without permission, carrying nothing but the fact that you went. It will mean everything to some and nothing to those who count such things differently.

choices.text: Stay with the army. The vow was impossible.
choices.result: You turn away from the hill. The men who went do not come back for two days. Some do not come back at all. You are whole and fed and you have followed orders. You will have years to decide if that was enough.

choices.text: Wait here for Richard's final decision.
choices.result: You wait. The decision is made by men with more power than you. You neither go nor refuse. When the army turns for Jaffa, you turn with it.

events.title: Ayyadieh. Richard has ordered the execution of the 2,700 Acre garrison prisoners — negotiations over the True Cross have collapsed, the army must march, and the prisoners cannot be moved or released. The order passes down the ranks. You are expected to participate.

text.default: You stand in the line at Ayyadieh and you know what you are. You kept the prisoner at Acre. You drew a line. And now the man who drew that line is being ordered to step across it by his king, in full view of God and the enemy and his own company. The thing that makes this unbearable is not doubt — it is clarity. You know exactly what the vow said. You know exactly what this is. You do it, or you do not. Either way, something that cannot be given back is gone before the sun sets.

The thing that makes this unbearable is not doubt — it is clarity. You know exactly what the vow said. You know exactly what this is. You do it, or you do not. Either way, something that cannot be given back is gone before the sun sets.

You stand in the line at Ayyadieh and you find that it is not as far from the scout at Acre as you might have hoped. The same logic. The same weight. The same answer. You are a man who does what the crusade requires. You have been that man for some time now. You lift your sword and you are not surprised by yourself, and that is the most frightening thing — that you are not surprised.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Master Bertrand
sages.title: Crusader Siege Engineer
sages.bio: Master Bertrand oversees the mangonels and siege towers outside Acre. He has built and broken walls from Sicily to Cyprus. He does not pray much but he understands force and leverage with the devotion of a churchman.
sages.greeting: The engineer squints at the wall, then at you. 'You want to know how to take a city? Come look at this stone. Every wall has a weakness if you know where to push.'
sages.advice: 'Acre has held two years because nobody committed fully. Half-measures kill more men than sieges do. You want to go home? Help me put this mangonel in the right place tonight.'

question.question: What was the main military purpose of a mangonel at a medieval siege?
choices: Carry soldiers over walls on a platform
Hurl heavy stones at walls and defenders
Dig tunnels beneath city foundations
Block enemy supply ships in harbour
question.explanation: Mangonels were stone-throwing siege engines that battered walls and demoralized defenders. At Acre, crusaders used mangonels to chip away at the walls while disease and supply shortages wore down both sides.
question.teksRef: WH.9(A) — Medieval military technology and siege warfare

sages.name: Richard I of England
sages.title: King of England, Commander of the Crusade
sages.bio: Richard I — called Coeur de Lion, the Lionheart — led the Third Crusade with a combination of personal recklessness and tactical genius. He took Acre, won at Arsuf, and twice turned back from Jerusalem when he judged the logistics impossible. His greatest general skill was keeping a fractious coalition moving forward.
sages.greeting: The king looks up from a map weighted with stones. 'A knight with a question. Ask it quickly — I have three other problems before Vespers.'
sages.advice: 'Discipline is the only thing standing between this army and a rabble. Hold the line even when it costs you. Especially when it costs you. That is what the cross means — not pilgrimage, not glory. Discipline.'

question.question: Why did Richard twice approach Jerusalem but refuse to attack it?
choices: He secretly made a truce with Saladin before the march
His army was too small to hold the city after capturing it
Philip II of France ordered him to return home
The Pope forbade an assault on the holy city
question.explanation: Richard calculated that even if the crusaders stormed Jerusalem, they lacked the garrison strength to hold it once the main army departed. Taking a city you cannot keep would be worse than the compromise peace he ultimately accepted.
question.teksRef: WH.9(B) — Causes and consequences of the Crusades

sages.name: Al-Adil Sayf ad-Din (Saphadin)
sages.title: Saladin's Brother and Diplomatic Envoy
sages.bio: Al-Adil was Saladin's younger brother, his most trusted general, and the Ayyubid dynasty's chief negotiator with the crusaders. He dealt directly with Richard I across lines of war with a pragmatism and occasional warmth that surprised both sides. The Treaty of Jaffa was largely his work.
sages.greeting: The envoy dismounts without armour, his interpreter stepping forward. 'Your king and my brother are very similar men. It has made this war very long. Perhaps we can end it before it makes orphans of everyone.'
sages.advice: 'Your vow brought you here. My brother's duty keeps him here. Neither of us will see Jerusalem surrendered. But pilgrims may walk there in peace if the swords are sheathed. That is worth more than a city no one can hold.'

question.question: What did the Treaty of Jaffa of 1192 actually accomplish?
choices: It returned Jerusalem to Christian rule for fifty years
It allowed Christian pilgrims to visit Jerusalem without military conquest
It expelled all Muslims from the Holy Land for a generation
It made Richard I the King of Jerusalem
question.explanation: The Treaty of Jaffa, signed in September 1192 between Richard and Saladin through Al-Adil's diplomacy, left Jerusalem under Muslim control but guaranteed Christian pilgrims safe access to the holy sites. It ended the Third Crusade without a military victory for either side.
question.teksRef: WH.9(B) — Outcomes and legacy of the Crusades

verdict.good: You held to the vow when it was inconvenient, when it cost you silver, sleep, and the approval of men who chose differently. That discipline did not take Jerusalem — nothing took Jerusalem. The Treaty of Jaffa gave pilgrims a road to the city and left the city in Saladin's hands. You came home from a war that did not win what it swore to win, carrying less silver than you left with and more knowledge of what men do to each other in God's name. You can say what you stood for. Not many who made that crossing can.
verdict.bad: Every time the choice came, you took the one that served you — a fuller purse, a rested body, the easy side of the line. You were not the worst man on the crusade; that distinction belongs to others, some of whom you watched. But you came to the Holy Land under a vow, and you spent that vow like coin, trading it for comfort wherever comfort was offered. The Treaty of Jaffa ended the war without Jerusalem. You were there for three years of killing and came home no poorer and no better. The men who held the line — and the men who died on the other side of it — deserved more from you than they got.
verdict.indifferent: You passed through the Third Crusade the way water passes through a hand — present, accounted for, leaving no mark. When the choices were hard you found the middle path, the sensible answer, the thing that offended no one and committed you to nothing. The siege of Acre, the massacre at Ayyadieh, the hill from which Jerusalem was visible and then not — these things happened around you. You survived them. Saladin kept the city. Richard sailed home in chains and was ransomed. The men who chose sides — on every side — at least chose. You were there. History will not record where you stood, because you made certain it could not.

data.reviewSummary:
The Third Crusade began in response to Saladin — Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, Sultan of Egypt and Syria — recapturing Jerusalem in 1187. Richard I of England and Philip II of France led the crusading host east, arriving at the siege of Acre, which had already ground on for two years. Both sides suffered terribly; dysentery and fever killed more crusaders than Saracen arrows, and mangonels hurled stones at the walls day and night. Acre fell on 12 July 1191. Shortly after, Philip II departed for France, leaving Richard in sole command. Then came the most debated act of the campaign: Richard ordered the execution of roughly 2,700 Acre garrison prisoners at Ayyadieh after ransom negotiations over the True Cross collapsed and the army needed to march south.

Richard's coastal march from Acre toward Jaffa became a model of medieval military discipline. He held his knights in tight formation under constant Saracen provocation, refusing to let anyone break rank to chase the Ayyubid cavalry. At the Battle of Arsuf in September 1191, the Hospitaller knights finally broke formation under pressure, forcing Richard to order a general charge — which won the battle decisively. The crusaders reached Jaffa and pressed inland.

Richard came within sight of Jerusalem twice and turned back both times. He judged, correctly, that his army could storm the city but could not hold it once the crusade disbanded and the soldiers went home. Taking Jerusalem without the strength to keep it would have been worse than the compromise he ultimately made.

That compromise was the Treaty of Jaffa, signed in September 1192, brokered largely by Al-Adil — Saladin's brother, known to the crusaders as Saphadin. The treaty left Jerusalem under Muslim control but guaranteed Christian pilgrims safe access to the holy sites. It ended three years of war without a military victory for either side. Richard sailed home in October 1192, was captured by the Duke of Austria, and was held for ransom. Conrad of Montferrat, the rival claimant to the Kingdom of Jerusalem whose political friction had complicated the campaign throughout, had already been assassinated earlier that year.

data.title: ROUTE 66
data.subtitle: Oklahoma to California, 1936
data.introBody: Spring, 1936. The bank took the farm. You've loaded your family into a rattling '28 Chevy and pointed it west. California is rumored to have work. Every decision costs something.
data.trailFeedOpener: The truck idles on the dirt road outside what used to be your farm. The kids are quiet. Your wife watches the house until it disappears.

paces.label: Easy
paces.desc: Rest the engine, watch the temperature gauge.

paces.label: Steady
paces.desc: Standard driving — cover ground without pushing it.

paces.label: Push
paces.desc: Drive hard, skip rests — the desert doesn't forgive this.

events.title: Somewhere on Route 66 in New Mexico, the radiator has blown and the family has pulled off the road in punishing heat. Grandpa is too sick to go on without rest. A younger brother — nineteen years old, strong, impatient — says he is going to catch a ride ahead with a passing family to scout work in the San Joaquin Valley and send money back when he finds it. He means it. He is not running. But once he climbs into that truck, the road and the distance will do what they do.
events.text: Your brother stands at the truck door, pack in hand, waiting for you to say something. Grandpa is gray-faced in the wagon bed behind you. Your mother's eyes are on you because you are the one who has kept the count of heads at every camp. The truck driver is not going to wait all afternoon. What do you say?

choices.text: You block the truck door with your body. 'We came out of Oklahoma as one family and we go into California the same way. Wait for Grandpa. Wait for all of us.' Your brother's jaw tightens, but he stays.
choices.result: The player has claimed the role of keeper — the one who holds the circle closed even when the circle costs. They have made family an obligation that overrides individual need, including their brother's need, including perhaps their own. They will be the person others lean on and the person who cannot let go.

choices.text: You step aside. You hand him what little cash you can spare and say, 'Send word when you land somewhere.' You watch the truck pull back onto the highway and you do not call after it.
choices.result: The player has acknowledged that love does not always mean holding on — that the family was already changing shape on this road and they chose not to lie about it. They will carry the gap where their brother was, and they will live with what that gap means about who they became when it mattered.

events.title: Black Blizzard at the Texas Line
events.text: A wall of brown-black dust rolls in from the north — one of the 'black blizzards' that have been burying farms across the Panhandle since 1934. You can't see the hood ornament. The family pulls their shirts over their faces.
trivia: Dust storms in the 1930s could bury fence posts and suffocate livestock overnight.
The Dust Bowl was caused by drought AND years of overplowing that stripped prairie grasses holding the soil.

choices.text: Pull over and wait it out under blankets.
choices.result: The family huddles together. The kids cough but they're all right. The truck is better for the rest.

choices.text: Keep driving slow — staying ahead of it.

outcomes.result: Dust clogs the air filter. You pull over anyway and spend an hour cleaning it out.
You push through. The engine sounds rough, but you're moving.

choices.text: Find a farmhouse and ask to shelter.

outcomes.result: A farm family — just as broke as you — shares cornbread and lets you wait it out. Strangers helping strangers.
The farmer asks for two dollars for the shelter. You pay it. You'd have done the same.

events.title: Radiator Trouble in the Heat
events.text: Steam hisses from under the hood fifty miles into New Mexico. The truck's overheating. A roadside garage — hand-painted sign, one pump — is two hundred yards ahead. The mechanic eyes the truck the way a buzzard eyes a sick cow.
trivia: Okie migrants were often cheated by roadside mechanics who knew a broken-down family had no choice.
Many families carried spare parts and tools because professional repairs could wipe out their remaining cash.

choices.text: Pay whatever he asks. We can't be stranded.
choices.result: Eight dollars. Probably worth four. The radiator is fixed and the engine sounds better. You swallow it.

choices.text: Negotiate hard. Offer five dollars flat.

outcomes.result: He grumbles but takes it. You saved three dollars and kept the truck running.
He patches it fast and cheap. It'll hold for now — maybe.

choices.text: Fix it yourself with the spare hose in the bed.

outcomes.result: It takes two hours in the heat but the hose holds. Your oldest watches and learns something.
Wrong fitting. The patch fails ten miles down the road. You end up paying the mechanic anyway.

events.title: Camp at the Pecos River Bridge
events.text: Dozens of families are camped along the riverbank — Okies, Texans, Arkansawyers, all pointed west. A family three tents over hasn't eaten today. Their truck blew a rod outside Amarillo and they've been here four days waiting for a part.
trivia: Roadside migrant camps sprang up wherever travelers broke down or ran out of gas — informal communities of shared hardship.
California passed laws in 1936 trying to turn back Okie migrants at the state line, though enforcement was inconsistent.

choices.text: Share some cornmeal from the larder box.
choices.result: The mother thanks you without words. Your own kids watch you share what little you have. Your wife says nothing, but she counts what's left.

choices.text: Offer a dollar toward their truck part.
choices.result: You can't spare much but you spare a dollar. They add it to what they've already collected from three other families.

choices.text: Keep to your camp. You can't feed everyone.
choices.result: Your wife makes supper without comment. The kids eat. The family three tents over goes to bed without.

choices.text: Ask if they know road conditions west of here.
choices.result: They know about a detour that saves you twenty miles and a toll bridge. A fair trade — information for a little company.

events.title: The Mojave Waits
events.text: You've reached the Arizona-California border. The desert ahead is unforgiving — 120 degrees in the truck cab, and it's only June. Every mile you push is a mile the engine runs hot.
events.leaveText: Find shade and rest until the worst heat breaks.

attempts.buttonText: Drive the early morning hours while it's cool.
attempts.successText: Three good hours before the heat climbs. The truck handles it.
attempts.failureText: A tire blows on the hot asphalt. Spare is on, but it costs time and sweat.

attempts.buttonText: Push through the midday heat — no stopping.
attempts.successText: The engine protests but holds. You're past the worst of it.
attempts.failureText: The engine seizes in the midday heat. It takes three hours and your last dollars to sort it out.

attempts.buttonText: Drive through the night to beat the heat entirely.
attempts.successText: The stars are something. You roll into Needles at dawn with a cool engine and the family asleep in the bed.
attempts.failureText: You fall asleep at the wheel at 2 a.m. The truck goes into the shoulder. No one's hurt, but the front axle is bent.

events.title: The California Line
events.text: A California Highway Patrol checkpoint. The officer looks at the truck — your family, your load, your Oklahoma plates — and asks how much money you're carrying. The 'bum blockade' is real: California tried to turn back migrants it called 'indigent.'
trivia: In 1936 the Los Angeles Police Department sent 136 officers to California's borders to turn back Okie migrants — the 'bum blockade,' declared unconstitutional in 1941.
California's agricultural valleys needed the labor migrants provided, but towns and counties resisted the social cost of feeding them.

choices.text: Show the cash you have. Answer honestly.

outcomes.result: He waves you through with a long look. You're legal — barely.
He turns you back to a 'registration tent' where someone collects a 'processing fee.' You pay and get through.

choices.text: Tell him you have family waiting with work arranged.

outcomes.result: He can't verify it. He lets you through.
He doesn't believe you, but he takes two dollars and waves you on. Your wife heard the lie.

choices.text: Know your rights — this blockade is unconstitutional.
choices.result: He argues. You hold your ground. After ten minutes he waves you through, looking for easier targets. Your hands are still shaking.

events.title: The Labor Contractor's Terms
events.text: Outside Bakersfield a labor contractor stands at a folding table, clipboard in hand. Cotton picking. Fifteen cents per hundredweight. Housing provided — company tent row, rent deducted from wages. A hundred families are lined up behind you. He doesn't need to negotiate.
trivia: San Joaquin Valley cotton pickers in 1936 earned as little as 15 cents per hundredweight — deliberately kept low by contractors who overcrowded the labor pool with desperate migrants.
Company housing deducted from wages was a near-exact replay of the tenant farming system many Okies had just escaped.

choices.text: Sign on. Any work is work.
choices.result: You sign. The work is brutal and the pay is less than promised after deductions. But the family eats this week.

choices.text: Refuse his terms and ask other migrants to hold out too.
choices.result: A few families hold with you. The contractor calls in replacements. Most go hungry another two days — but three families hold the line and win twenty cents instead.

choices.text: Negotiate alone for better wages.

outcomes.result: He bumps you to eighteen cents — quietly, so the others don't see. Your family eats; the family next to you doesn't know what rate you got.
He shakes his head and calls the next family up. You take the fifteen cents anyway.

events.title: Arriving at the labor camp outside Bakersfield, the family is registered by a camp manager who asks how many in your party. You give your count.

text.default: You give every name, including your brother's. You tell the manager he is coming behind you. You have said this at every camp since New Mexico — 'he is coming behind us' — and you believe it less each time, but you cannot bring yourself to strike his name. Other families here have done the same arithmetic you have refused to do. You do not speak to them about it.

variants.text: You give every name, including your brother's. You tell the manager he is coming behind you. You have said this at every camp since New Mexico — 'he is coming behind us' — and you believe it less each time, but you cannot bring yourself to strike his name. Other families here have done the same arithmetic you have refused to do. You do not speak to them about it.

You give the number as it stands now. The manager writes it down without looking up. It is the first time you have said the count aloud since New Mexico, and the number sits in your chest like a stone. Around you, other families arrive still whole, or pretending to be. You do not envy them exactly. You just know the road made a certain kind of person out of you, and you are not yet sure what to do with that.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: John Steinbeck
sages.title: Journalist & Novelist
sages.bio: In 1936 Steinbeck wrote 'The Harvest Gypsies' for the San Francisco News — seven dispatches on migrant life that shocked readers and influenced New Deal policy. He was in the camps, watching, before he wrote 'The Grapes of Wrath.'
sages.greeting: A man with a notebook approaches your camp outside Albuquerque. He doesn't look like a reporter — he's dusty and quiet — but he asks careful questions and writes down what you say.
sages.advice: He says: 'People need to see your face, not a number. A photograph and a story will do more for relief funding than any petition.' He's writing it down right now.

question.question: What was the primary structural cause of the Dust Bowl, beyond drought alone?
choices: Railroad companies had rerouted rivers for profit
Years of deep plowing destroyed the prairie grasses that held the soil
The federal government banned crop rotation in the 1920s
Cattle had eaten all the topsoil vegetation by 1930
question.explanation: Drought triggered the Dust Bowl, but decades of deep, single-crop plowing had already stripped the native grasses whose root systems anchored the topsoil. When the rain stopped, there was nothing to hold the soil down.
question.teksRef: 8.29(A) — Environmental and economic causes of the Great Depression era

portraitAttribution.artist: McFadden Publications, Inc.; no photographer credited; photo likely the work of Sonya Noskowiak, as Steinbeck is wearing the same clothes from her 1935 studio session that produced the work shown here: https://www.si.edu/object/npg_NPG.2006.74

sages.name: Dorothea Lange
sages.title: FSA Photographer
sages.bio: Lange was hired by the Farm Security Administration to document migrant conditions across California. Her photographs — including 'Migrant Mother,' taken in 1936 — became the defining images of the Depression and forced Congress to act on relief funding.
sages.greeting: A woman with a large camera waits outside the camp water tap. She asks if she can photograph your family. She says the pictures go to the federal government.
sages.advice: She says: 'I don't want to capture poverty. I want to capture the dignity that poverty can't take from a person.' She photographs your hands, not your face, and you understand the difference.

question.question: How did Dorothea Lange's photographs affect Dust Bowl migrants?
choices: They were used by California officials to turn migrants away
They were published widely and increased federal pressure to fund migrant relief
They documented crop yields for the Department of Agriculture
They were kept classified until the 1950s
question.explanation: Lange's FSA photographs were distributed to newspapers and magazines nationwide. The public response created political pressure on Congress to expand New Deal relief programs for migrants — making her camera a tool of policy change.
question.teksRef: 8.29(B) — Role of media and public awareness in New Deal policy responses

sages.name: Tom Collins
sages.title: FSA Camp Manager, Shafter CA
sages.bio: Tom Collins managed the federal Farm Security Administration migrant camps at Visalia and Shafter, California. He kept meticulous records, lobbied local authorities on migrants' behalf, and became a trusted figure to the families who passed through. Steinbeck used Collins's reports as source material.
sages.greeting: The man at the intake desk of the Shafter FSA camp looks tired in the good way — the way of someone who has cared about something for a long time. He shakes your hand and asks your family's names. All of them.
sages.advice: He says: 'The camp has a doctor on Tuesdays and a school tent every morning. You earn your stay with a few hours of maintenance work. No charity — a deal between equals.' You haven't been spoken to like that in a long time.

question.question: What did the Farm Security Administration's migrant camps provide that most roadside camps did not?
choices: Armed guards to keep out California residents
Permanent housing and land grants
Clean water, medical care, and organized community governance
Train tickets back to Oklahoma
question.explanation: FSA camps — managed by people like Tom Collins — provided sanitation, medical access, and democratic camp councils where migrants governed their own rules. They were a sharp contrast to the squalid roadside camps where most migrants lived.
question.teksRef: 8.30(A) — New Deal programs and federal response to the Great Depression

A farmer who rented land and shared the crop with the landowner

eventTrivia.question: Why did California officials try to turn back Okie migrants at the border in 1936?
choices: Migrants carried diseases banned by federal law
California feared the social cost of supporting indigent arrivals
Route 66 had a legal toll controlled by California
Oklahoma migrants were not allowed to work in California under federal law
eventTrivia.fact: California counties feared migrants would require public relief. The LAPD 'bum blockade' of 1936 tried to turn back migrants labeled indigent — a practice later ruled unconstitutional.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Farm Security Administration (FSA) created to do?
choices: Buy up failed farms and resell them to banks
Provide loans, camps, and relief to displaced farm families
Build irrigation canals across California
Recruit migrants to work on federal construction projects
eventTrivia.fact: The FSA was a New Deal agency that built and ran sanitary migrant camps, provided loans to displaced farmers, and documented conditions through its photography program — including Dorothea Lange's work.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Soil Conservation Service created to address?
choices: Overproduction of wheat and corn in the Midwest
Soil erosion caused by poor land-use practices across the Great Plains
Flooding in the Mississippi River Delta
The collapse of cotton prices on world markets
eventTrivia.fact: Hugh Hammond Bennett's Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935, promoted contour plowing, windbreaks, and grassland restoration to prevent the kind of erosion that created the Dust Bowl.

eventTrivia.question: What highway did most Okie migrants follow west to California?
choices: Highway 1 along the Pacific Coast
Route 66 from Oklahoma through Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona
The Lincoln Highway through Nebraska and Nevada
Route 40 through Tennessee and Arkansas
eventTrivia.fact: Route 66 — running from Chicago to Los Angeles — passed directly through Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, making it the natural corridor for Dust Bowl migrants headed to California.

eventTrivia.question: How did falling cotton prices contribute to the Dust Bowl migration?
choices: Low prices forced farmers to plant more acres, exhausting the soil faster
Cotton prices rose, attracting too many new farmers
The federal government banned cotton farming in Oklahoma
Low prices caused banks to invest in Oklahoma farmland
eventTrivia.fact: When cotton prices collapsed in the late 1920s, tenant farmers tried to stay solvent by planting more acres. More plowing stripped more topsoil — setting the stage for the dust storms that followed.

eventTrivia.question: What did John Steinbeck's 1936 series 'The Harvest Gypsies' document?
choices: The working conditions of migrant farm laborers in California
The history of Route 66 construction
The federal soil conservation program in Oklahoma
The rise of labor unions among California cannery workers
eventTrivia.fact: Steinbeck's seven-part San Francisco News series described the living and working conditions of Okie migrants in California's fields — helping build public support for New Deal relief programs.

eventTrivia.question: What term did Californians use for Oklahoma and Texas migrants — often as a slur?
choices: Drifters
Boomers
Okies
Sooners

eventTrivia.question: What made a broken-down truck on Route 66 especially dangerous for migrant families?
choices: The truck was often the family's only home and only means of reaching work
Broken trucks were impounded by highway patrol
Parts stores refused to serve out-of-state travelers
Federal law required migrants to have working vehicles
eventTrivia.fact: Most migrant families had no alternative transport or shelter. A stranded truck meant no home, no way to reach work, and rapidly dwindling cash — a single breakdown could end the journey entirely.

eventTrivia.question: What was the crop-lien system that trapped many tenant farmers?

An arrangement where merchants advanced credit against the future harvest — often at exploitative rates
A law requiring farmers to store grain in federal silos
A railroad pricing scheme that set freight rates for crops
eventTrivia.fact: Under crop-lien, merchants advanced seed and supplies on credit, with the crop pledged as repayment. Interest rates were often crushing, keeping tenant farmers in perpetual debt even in good years.

eventTrivia.question: How many people are estimated to have migrated out of the Dust Bowl region in the 1930s?
choices: About 10,000
About 50,000
Roughly 2.5 million
Over 10 million
eventTrivia.fact: Historians estimate approximately 2.5 million people left the Great Plains states during the 1930s Dust Bowl migration — one of the largest internal migrations in American history.

eventTrivia.question: What did labor contractors do in California's agricultural valleys in the 1930s?
choices: They built company towns for permanent farm workers
They recruited and controlled migrant harvest workers, setting wages and housing terms

data.reviewSummary:
The Dust Bowl migration of the 1930s grew from two converging disasters. Decades of deep, single-crop plowing had stripped the native prairie grasses whose root systems held the Great Plains topsoil in place — when sustained drought hit after 1930, powerful winds carried the unanchored soil in massive storms called black blizzards. The worst, Black Sunday on April 14, 1935, turned noon to night across the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandle. Falling cotton prices had already pushed tenant farmers — sharecroppers who rented land and paid the landowner a share of the crop — into unpayable debt through the crop-lien system, where merchants advanced seed on credit at crushing interest rates. By the mid-1930s, approximately 2.5 million people had fled the Great Plains states, most following Route 66 through Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona toward California.

California met them with suspicion. In 1936 the Los Angeles Police Department sent 136 officers to the state's borders in a 'bum blockade,' turning back migrants labeled indigent — a practice later ruled unconstitutional. In the San Joaquin Valley, labor contractors recruited desperate migrants, set wages as low as fifteen cents per hundredweight, and provided company housing whose rent was deducted from already-thin paychecks — replicating the debt-and-dependency cycle many had fled. The word 'Okie,' originally for Oklahomans, became a slur applied to any Dust Bowl migrant.

Federal response came through the New Deal. Hugh Hammond Bennett's Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935, promoted contour plowing and grassland restoration to reverse the erosion that had made the Dust Bowl possible. The Farm Security Administration built and managed sanitary migrant camps providing clean water, medical care on rotating schedules, and democratic camp councils where migrants governed their own rules — a sharp contrast to roadside camps. Tom Collins managed FSA camps at Visalia and Shafter, California, keeping records and lobbying local authorities on migrants' behalf. Dorothea Lange, hired by the FSA, photographed migrant conditions; her 1936 image 'Migrant Mother' was distributed to newspapers nationwide and drove congressional pressure to expand relief funding. John Steinbeck's 1936 San Francisco News series 'The Harvest Gypsies' documented farmworker conditions and shaped public opinion ahead of 'The Grapes of Wrath.'
